learningObjective: Determine whether two adjacent loops with a producer-consumer dependence can be legally fused into a single loop nest.
stem: The proposed fusion above tries to combine a producer loop and a consumer loop into one. Is the fused loop semantically equivalent to the original, and why?

options.text: No — inside iteration `i`, the fused body reads `B[i+1]`, which has not been produced yet by iteration `i+1`; the fusion violates the flow dependence from producer to consumer.
Yes — because both loops have the same trip count `N`, fusion is always legal regardless of the access pattern.
Yes — because the two original loops iterate in the same order, fusion preserves semantics as long as all reads and writes touch the same array.
No — fusion is illegal because the two loops write to different arrays (`B` and `C`); fusion requires the write target to be identical.

explanation: The classic legality condition for loop fusion is that no fused iteration can require a value that would be produced by a later iteration of the fused loop (no forward-crossing flow dependence). Here, iteration `i` needs `B[i+1]`, which is only defined by iteration `i+1` in the producer loop. In the fused loop, iteration `i+1` has not yet run when iteration `i` executes, so `B[i+1]` is either stale or uninitialized. Same trip count is necessary but not sufficient. Writing to different arrays is a normal fusion case, not a blocker.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: forward-crossing flow dependence violates fusion legality.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: identical trip count is necessary but not sufficient — cross-iteration dependences can still be violated.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: same iteration order does not save fusion when a later iteration's value is needed.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: writing to different arrays is normal for fusion; it is the dependence structure that matters.

assumptions: Boundary conditions for `i=0` and `i=N-1` are handled or ignored for this analysis.
`f` and `g` are pure functions of their inputs.
nonImplications: Does not imply the fusion is unrecoverable; a shift/peel or 2-iteration lookahead buffer can restore legality.
